title: In 1949 an economist built a computer that modelled an economy with coloured water

cover.alt: A black-and-white photo of economist Bill Phillips standing beside his tall MONIAC machine of clear tanks and tubes.

body: The **MONIAC**, or Phillips Machine, is an analogue computer in which money is water. The New Zealand economist Bill Phillips built the first one in 1949, while a student at the London School of Economics, with help from Walter Newlyn, in his landlady's garage in Croydon. Coloured water flows from a treasury tank into spending, savings drain some of it away, investment adds some back, and taxes pump it back up to the treasury. Turning taps and pumps sets things like tax rates, and you can watch the whole economy adjust. Phillips and Newlyn found it could be calibrated to an accuracy of 2%.

steps.label: Water starts in the treasury tank
It flows out into spending, like health
Savings drain some off; investment adds some
Taxes pump water back to the treasury

slides.question: How much did Phillips spend building the first machine, in 1949 pounds?
slides.explanation: £400, about £12,000 in 2025 money, for a machine built in a garage.

slides.heading: Why plumbing?
slides.text: The name is a pun on money and ENIAC, an early electronic computer. Instead of equations on paper, the machine shows money building up as savings, leaving the country as imports or arriving as exports, and what a change at one tap does to every other tank.

slides.heading: Where they went
slides.text: Roughly 12 to 14 were built. Buyers included Harvard Business School and Melbourne University. Machines survive at the Science Museum in London, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Museum and Cambridge's Faculty of Economics, where one has been restored to working order.

slides.question: In Terry Pratchett's novel Making Money, what happens to a similar machine once it is perfected?
options: It becomes linked to the real economy
It is sold to a bank
slides.explanation: In the Discworld story the machine becomes magically linked to the economy it models, so changing the water changes real money.
